scenarios.title: Spicy food, revised
scenarios.summary: A preference changes. The old value is retired to history, not deleted, and never shown again.

turns.text: I love spicy food, the hotter the better.
Spicy food doesn't agree with me any more.
Any dinner ideas?

scenarios.title: Avoids seafood, loves sushi
scenarios.summary: A narrower preference is an exception, not a contradiction: both are kept and the specific one wins.

turns.text: I avoid seafood.
Sushi is the exception though, I love it.
Any dinner ideas?

scenarios.title: A later, broader statement
scenarios.summary: When a broad statement comes after the exception, OntoMem keeps both but asks before relying on the exception.

turns.text: I avoid seafood, but I love sushi.
No seafood at all for me now.
What should I eat tonight?

scenarios.title: Paris: memory vs plan
scenarios.summary: A past experience and a future plan about the same place are different slots - no conflict.

turns.text: We loved our Paris trip last year!
Planning to go back to Paris next summer.
Any trip ideas?

scenarios.title: My wife hates mushrooms
scenarios.summary: Statements about other people go into their own slots and never overwrite the user's.

turns.text: I love mushrooms.
My wife hates mushrooms though.
What should I cook for my wife?

scenarios.title: Spicy food vs spicy thrillers
scenarios.summary: Similar words, different slots. A surface-matching memory would merge these; the ontology does not.

turns.text: Spicy food doesn't agree with me.
I'm really into spicy thrillers lately.
What should I watch tonight?

scenarios.title: Coffee at work, not at home
scenarios.summary: The same concept can be liked in one context and avoided in another.

turns.text: At home, I avoid coffee.
At work I love coffee.
What should I get for a work lunch?

scenarios.title: Going vegan
scenarios.summary: One identity statement expands into several hard constraints that veto whole branches of the catalog.

turns.text: I love butter chicken and cheese.
I'm vegan now.
Any dinner ideas?
